title: The work list
eyebrow: What is being worked on, what is finished, and what is waiting on somebody
dek: The one register this archive did not have. Findings go to the searched log, errors to the corrections, unanswered questions to the open questions, missing people to the gaps, and letters to the errands — but what we are actually going to do next lived only in the conversation, which is the one place that does not survive.
lead:
Every other register here answers *«what do we know?»*. This one answers *«what is being done?»*, and it exists because that question was being carried in a chat window.

**The twenty open items are at the top, in the order a reader should take them.** Below them is what is finished, and what was struck for being founded on a mistake — kept and struck through rather than deleted, the same way this archive treats a retracted claim.

**Five states, and an owner on every row.** *Running* means somebody or something is at it now. *Next* means it is ready to start. *Blocked* means it waits on a person or an institution, and the **owner** says which. The dates are there so that something blocked for five weeks does not read like something raised this morning.

rows.what: The ark harvest — finished
rows.note: **Done on 15 September: 5,482 of 5,482 volumes are linkable, and not one is outstanding.** The harvester ran 2,359 waypoint calls in David's Chrome without a single failure after it was restarted. **Senj was the case David raised** — fifteen volumes across three parishes with no link on any of them; all fifteen are openable now.

rows.what: Ovaro «Matrimoni, allegati» 1807 — the cheapest thing on this list
rows.note: **Read. No De Franceschi — and a better finding than the one it was opened for.** The file came up from **Capodistria**: banns published in Istria, a mother's consent notarised there, and the folded letter from one civil office to the other. [What it means](/carnia/#ovaro1807) is that **Istrian paper sits inside Carnian marriage files** — which is why the thirteen unread Mione allegati just became the most valuable shelf in the archive.

rows.what: Read the Mione and Ovaro «Matrimoni, allegati» — the best shelf in the archive
rows.note:
**Three read, nineteen to go.** Each of the three has given up something the registers alone could not:

**Mione 1806** — [Gio: Batta and Osvaldo De' Franceschi](/carnia/#allegati1806), two generations in one sheet, with the Pieve's seal still on it.
**Mione 1815** — [Pietro De Franceschi](/carnia/#allegati1815), Felice Santo's grandfather.
**Ovaro 1807** — [a file that came up from Capodistria](/carnia/#ovaro1807), proving the series also carries Istrian paper.

**An allegato is the only place the lost Pieve di Gorto register speaks.** Twelve Mione volumes and seven Ovaro ones remain.

That is a block on the connection and not the eight-kilobyte cookie this archive diagnosed in September. Worth retrying later or from another network; nothing else about the reading has changed.

rows.what: The eight remaining Mione «Morti», 1806–1815
rows.note:
[Morti 1810 is read](/carnia/#morti1810) and gave four deaths of the surname, a son in minor orders, and «Erman De Franceschi» in a man's own signature. Eight volumes left. **A Pietro De Franceschi dying in his seventies settles the question the 1792 extract opened**, and from 1813 each volume ends with a «Tavola Alfabetica» that makes it a page rather than a book.

rows.note:
**Mieli turned up by accident** — its arks sit immediately before Mione's, which is how the one-comune-per-block assumption was caught. The Val di Gorto has a dozen comuni and this archive has catalogued three. A De Franceschi who left Mione did not necessarily leave the valley.

rows.what: Bring in the rest of the living family, name only
rows.note: **Done, and the rule changed under it.** All eleven living people the archive names are placed — eight at Johannesburg, five at Brisbane, two in both — and eight more came in from the tree on 15–16 September: **Lidija, Peter, Renata and Ursula** of the Crikvenica and German households, and the Australian branch. **Twenty-six living people, and the build gate confirms zero dates reach any page.**

rows.what: Settle whether «Erman» is a by-name on a De Franceschi house
rows.note: **Struck the day it was raised.** The question was whether *Erman* is a by-name on a De Franceschi house. It is not: his **1809 marriage act**, already in this archive, gives him as son of the late **Pietro Erman** and **Maddalena née de Franceschi**. The compound is his two parents. [Logged](/corrections/).

rows.what: Valentina or Cattarina — one wife renamed, or two wives in turn?
rows.note:
The marriage index calls Osvaldo's wife **Valentina Prencis** on 6 August 1807. The birth act calls her **Cattarina nata Crencis** on 15 October 1810. Both readings are held open. The Mione «Morti» would settle it if the first one died.

rows.what: Daniele «del fu Osvaldo» de Canova — brother of the bride, or a second Osvaldo?
rows.note:
He witnesses Lucia Santa's wedding in 1815 and the act calls all four witnesses *«non parenti, né affini»*. Her father was **Osvaldo Antonio de Caneva**; Daniele, forty-nine, was born about 1766. **Either two Osvaldos at Liariis, or the formula is boilerplate.**

rows.what: Send the Pieve di Santa Maria di Gorto enquiry
rows.note: **The single most valuable letter this archive has ever drafted.** Mione's civil births stop at 1810 and there is no civil registration at all before 1806 — so Paolo, Osvaldo, Francesco, Matteo, Felice Santo **and now Pietro** were all baptised in a book only Gorto holds. [The draft is written, in Italian, and ready to send](/errands/).

rows.what: The three archive request forms that need David's own data
rows.note: DAPA has answered twice — for **Svetvinčenat** and **Pićan** — and both times asked for the same completed form: applicant's details, delivery address, billing details including an OIB. A third sits with **DAZD**. **This archive does not hold that data and will not invent it.**

rows.what: One Y-DNA reading from a male-line De Franceschi who is not Ivan's descendant
rows.note: **L-M27 rests on a father and a son, which is the same opinion asked twice.** One cousin reading his paternal haplogroup off an account he already has settles it either way. [The message is drafted](/dna/#settle); the Gračišće reunion families are the first ask.

rows.what: Turn the volumes nobody has filmed into named requests
rows.note:
**Done, and it was done before this row was raised.** [The undigitised](/undigitised/) sets the forty-nine out place by place and holder by holder with the DAPA shelf numbers, and carries **a draft request in Croatian** with the blanks named — the DAPA number and the years are what the office works from. `out/dapa-zahtjevi.md` carries the filled-in guidance for the two forms.

**What is left is not writing but sending**, and that waits on David's own details, like every other DAPA form.

rows.what: Track which volumes have been read, not just which places
rows.note: **Done: `site/src/data/reads.json`.** A row names a place, a volume in the words the panel prints, a state — **read** or **part** — and what was read. The builder stamps it onto the volume and **reports any row that matches no volume** rather than dropping it, which is how the Vodnjan title was caught wrong on the first run. Four volumes pinned so far; six places now have a book of their own opened.

rows.what: Find the Evangelical root in FamilySearch's waypoint tree
rows.note: **Found, walked and catalogued on 15 September.** The collection's own waypoint list names it — ten confession roots, and «Evangelical (Evangelička crkva)» is sd_4, waypoint `9R27-7M4:391644401`. **Six parishes, seven volumes**, all now catalogued with their arks harvested and openable from the map. **Brekinjska and Hrastovac stop being grey**, and every grey marker left on the map is a checked negative rather than an admission. [On the search register](/searched/).

rows.what: Widen the cross-provider check beyond six places
rows.note:
**Done, and it widened by a different route than expected.** The note said better name matching would turn one finding into forty. It did not need to: **the providers multiplied instead**, and the test now stands at **27 places** against six — Istria against Pazin, Međimurje against the Slovenian collection, Croatian Istria against the Italian one, Delnice against the main Croatian shelf. **294 volumes before 1890 listed by one holder and unfilmed by the other; 393 after 1890, which is privacy and not a hole.**

**And it was wrong in the other direction first.** The library catalogue had crept into the comparison, which inflated it to 78 places and 1,572 volumes — a bibliographic line spanning three centuries being read as a claim about a particular year. `fs-cat` is now excluded from the test, because a catalogue is not a shelf.

rows.what: Trieste AB and HB on Matricula — a shelf nobody on this estate has opened
rows.note: Looking for Croatia on Matricula found none, but it found **two Austrian Protestant congregations at Trieste**. Not this family's confession and no De Franceschi is known in either — but the Littoral archives overlap, and if another archive on the estate works Trieste this belongs to them.

rows.what: The 404 page that stops every publish
rows.note: `./scripts/publish.sh` builds and audits clean — **1,231 pages, every link and anchor** — then fails on **`MISSING OUTPUT: /404/`** and refuses to push. An untracked `404.astro` builds to `404.html` rather than `404/index.html`. It belongs to the session that owns the cross-site UI. **Everything here is being committed and pushed by hand around it.**

rows.what: The priority arks — clickable registers for our own parishes
rows.note: 425 volumes in the Istrian and Kvarner parishes this family is documented in, each now opening at page one from the [research map](/map/).

rows.what: Re-cut the research map's colour scale to depth
rows.note: **Struck: it answered a question nobody was asking.** Shading by how many volumes sit on a shelf looked better than the saturated three-state scale it replaced, and said less — **a parish with forty volumes nobody has opened and a parish with two nobody has opened are in the same state.** The colour now says *how far we have got*: never opened, started, read right through. Depth moved into the panel, in words, where it can sit next to «nobody has read any of it» without pretending to be it.

rows.what: Antenati as a fourth provider
rows.note: [Seventy-four volumes](/antenati/) for Mione, Ovaro and Mieli, every one verified by fetching its own catalogue page. Its arks sit on a different host from everything else, so the map sends a reader to the archive's own list rather than dressing them as FamilySearch links.

rows.what: Matricula Online as a fifth provider — Senj and Karlobag
rows.note: **Matricula holds no Croatian parish at all.** Twelve countries in its fonds index and Croatia is not one of them; its place search returns nothing for Senj, Karlobag, Rijeka or Fiume. The line was written from memory and never checked. [Logged as a correction](/corrections/).

rows.what: Cross-provider gap detection
rows.note: Six places are described by more than one provider, and they are the only places a gap can be seen. **147 volumes are listed at Pazin, from before 1890, that FamilySearch has not filmed** — and 313 more after 1890 that are the privacy cut-off and not a gap at all.

rows.what: The Ovaro marriage allegati for 1815
rows.note: **The best single hour of the day.** Felice Santo's baptismal extract of 2 November 1792 names *«Pauli filii Petri De Franceschi mionensis»* — [a grandfather this archive did not have](/carnia/#allegati1815) — copied out of the Pieve di Gorto's own register and certified at Luincis.

rows.what: Document the 1807 gap; draft the Pieve di Gorto enquiry
rows.note: Both. And [the gap turned out to be narrower than published](/carnia/#gap1807): Ovaro kept 1807, so it is one lost Mione volume rather than a hole in the system.

rows.what: The new people onto the roster
rows.note: Seventeen — from Felice Santo the weaver and Lucia Santa de Canova down to the two Luint tradesmen who witnessed a birth in 1810, and the priests who certified the extracts.

rows.what: Reconcile Brenci / Prencis / Crencis / Brenis / Brunis / Brencis
rows.note: [Six spellings, three women, one Friulian house-name](/carnia/#prences) — *«in cjasa da Prences»*. And a 1792 priest's Latin writes it **Prencis**, with a P, which is the earliest and most careful hand of the lot.

rows.what: Pazin's undigitised volumes as a letter list
rows.note: [The hundred and fifty-four](/undigitised/) — by place, by holder, with the DAPA shelf numbers and a draft in Croatian. **34 of them are in parishes on our own line.**

rows.what: Decided against: inferring Antenati volumes from ark ranges
rows.note: The first Antenati catalogue named fifty-nine volumes from contiguous ark ranges, assuming the portal numbers one comune at a time. **It does not** — an_ua667510 to 667513 are **Mieli**, a different comune, sitting immediately before Mione. Every volume is now fetched individually or it is not claimed. [Logged as a correction](/corrections/).

rows.what: The panel now groups the shelf by record type and names the gaps
rows.note:
A marker used to list its volumes in whatever order the providers were walked. It now shows a coverage timeline — Births, Marriages, Deaths — with every hole named and measured. **277 real gaps across 160 places**; 1,002 places have none.

A one- or two-year hole is called a labelling artefact rather than a loss, **except where every volume covers a single year** — the Napoleonic comuni — where a missing year is a missing book. That exception is what makes [Mione's lost 1807](/carnia/#gap1807) show as three gaps and not three shrugs.

rows.what: Each place shown under its older and other names
rows.note:
The «also written» line used to carry nothing but the catalogue's own noise — *«Fažana, Croatia»*. It now carries what the place was called when the register was written: **Rijeka as Fiume and Sankt Veit am Flaum, Pazin as Pisino, Gračišće as Gallignana, Svetvinčenat as Sanvincenti**. 609 of the 1,190 mapped places have one.

Taken from the GeoNames alternate-names column already held offline, with the airport codes, the Mandarin and Cyrillic romanisations, and the modern administrative wrappers («Grad Vodnjan») filtered out — and with spellings that are the same name without hačeks (*Fazhana*, *Svetvinchenat*) folded away rather than listed as identities.

rows.what: The three Pazin-hinterland parishes are absent from FamilySearch entirely
rows.note:
Checked against the full 1,333-parish walk of Croatia Church Books 2040054: **Gračišće, Gologorica and Pićan are not in it under any spelling** — nor Lindar, Beram, Trviž, Cerovlje, Zarečje, Grdoselo or Kašćerga. Boljun, Kršan and Kozljak are. **It is a patterned hole across the whole Pazin hinterland**, which is the ground this family comes off.

**Closed as answered rather than solved.** All **3,488** FamilySearch collections have since been walked and **none of them holds these parishes** — the hole is real and it is FamilySearch's, not a spelling problem. Gračišće, Gologorica and Pićan are at **Pazin and nowhere else**, which is why their 32, 22 and 4 volumes are catalogued and unopenable, and why they lead [the undigitised](/undigitised/). The next move is the DAPA request form, which is blocked on David's own data, not on more searching.

rows.what: The panel now colours the shelf by how far it has been read
rows.note:
**Green on what is done, red on the gaps, amber on what is part-done** — David's correction, applied to the panel as well as the marker.

A record-type heading turns **green** when every volume of that kind has been read, **amber** when some have, and stays plain when none have. Individual volumes go green when they have been read, in the collapsed list and in the clickable «open at page one» list alike. Gaps keep their red.

Mione now reads at a glance: **BIRTHS · ALL READ** in green, **MARRIAGES · 6 of 18 read** in amber, and **1807** in red three times over. All of it done from outside the shared Atlas component, which this session does not own.

rows.what: One volume shown four times in the panel — collapsed to one line
rows.note:
Meljani has a single register and the panel was showing it **four times**: as a record-type heading, as a coverage span, as a volume row, and again in the kit's own «open at page one» list.

**It is now one line**, with the link moved into the row it belongs to and the leftover list removed. The span row only appears where there is a gap to show; the fold only appears where there are more than four volumes. Done from outside the shared component, by matching the two lists on a label the builder deliberately makes identical.

rows.what: Harvest «Croatia, Delnice Deanery Catholic Church Books, 1571–1926»
rows.note: **Walked. Six reels, ~3,485 images, and no parish structure at all** — the collection browses by film number only. They hang on Delnice itself rather than pretending to a precision the collection does not have. **Which parishes each reel covers is a question for the catalogue record, not the browse tree.**

rows.what: Open «Austria, Catholic Church Records, 1565–2007» for the Austrian Littoral
rows.note:
**Struck: it does not cover the Littoral.** The collection has no browse tree — it is a name index of 6.85 million records — so it was searched instead. **289 Defranceschi inside it, every named place Tyrolean**: Bozen, Salorno, St. Florian. Three Istrian surnames tested beside it fall the same way.

**Gračišće, Gologorica and Pićan are not here**, and this was the best remaining candidate. [The negative is recorded in full](/searched/).

rows.what: Open «Hungary, Civil Registration, 1895–1980» for Fiume and the littoral
rows.note:
**Struck: Croatia-Slavonia never had Hungarian civil registration.** The collection browses by **33 Hungarian counties and not one Croatian one**, and there is no Fiume in it.

Hungary introduced civil registration in 1895; **Croatia-Slavonia kept the parish registers as the legal civil record until 1946**. So there is no Croatian civil registration to find — it was never created. [The negative, and why it explains Međimurje](/searched/).

rows.what: Put the places filed abroad on the map, under both names
rows.note:
**Done. 58 places, 409 volumes, 32 of them Croatian**, across three collections filed by Italy, Slovenia and Croatia-by-film.

An exonym table puts each on the same dot as its modern name — **Csáktornya→Čakovec, Perlak→Prelog, Buie→Buje** — with the catalogue's spelling kept in «also written», because that is the name you must search for.

**It found a gap on day one**: Čakovec is missing 1891–1894 in all three record types, the interval between the parish books closing and Hungarian civil registration opening. [Neither catalogue could show that alone](/elsewhere/).

rows.what: Walk every FamilySearch collection that could hold this family's ground
rows.note:
**Done, and it is exhaustive.** All **3,488** collections listed, every title read, and **44 opened** — every Croatian, Austrian, Hungarian and Slovenian one, plus the Italian collections for Gorizia, Trieste, Udine, Venezia, Belluno, Treviso, Padova, Verona and Vicenza.

**Five hold places on our ground and all five are now on the map. Thirty-nine hold nothing**, and each is [recorded as a negative](/collections-walk/) so nobody opens it twice.

**There is no Serbian, Bosnian, Montenegrin or Yugoslav collection at all**, and Croatia has exactly two.

rows.what: The Tyrolean Defranceschi — a second population of the surname
rows.note:
**It had a page already — [Trentino](/trentino/) — and what it was missing was the registers.** That page opened by saying every one of these people arrived through the family tree and **no register had ever been opened for any of them**. The Austrian collection walk had found **147 indexed entries, 1608 to 1915**, and nobody had put the two together.

**146 of the 147 are baptisms. 132 name both parents and 126 name a spouse** — more filiation than this archive holds for most of its own Istrian century. They are on the page now.

**And they sharpen the argument rather than softening it.** Nineteen in Carinthia and sixteen in South Tyrol is a scatter, not a cluster, and the surnames run *Franceschini* and *Franzeschini* — Italian names that reached Austria by a different road from the Istrian one. **A hundred and seven of the 147 carry no town at all**, which is the same index failure this archive already solved for Croatia by resolving the image ark to its film; that resolution has not been run here.

rows.what: Write up why Croatia has no civil registration before 1946
rows.note:
Two collection walks in one evening produced the same structural fact from opposite ends: **Hungary registered civilly from 1895 and Croatia-Slavonia did not**, keeping the parish books as the legal record until **1946**.

**Written and published on [the method page](/method/)**, where it belongs: the Nagodba of 1868 left Croatia-Slavonia its own administration, so Hungary's 1895 civil registration did not reach it and **the parish books stayed the legal civil record until 1946**. It explains why FamilySearch's Croatian collection is church books, why Pazin's list is parish registers, and why Međimurje is the exception — it was governed as part of Zala county, which is Hungary proper.

rows.what: Decide whether the 250 other Italian collections are worth walking
rows.note:
FamilySearch has **257 Italian collections**; the walk opened the nine that touch the Adriatic and the Veneto. The rest are Naples, Sicily, Piedmont, Puglia — **irrelevant to this family's ground, and squarely the business of the Falco and Mazza archives**.

**Decided against, and the reason is scope rather than effort.** Naples, Sicily, Piedmont and Puglia are not this family's ground in any century the archive can reach, and walking them would fill this map with a quarter of Italy to no purpose. The nine Adriatic and Veneto collections that could hold Istrian or Carnian material **have** been walked and are [on the collections walk](/collections-walk/).

**The list is worth handing over rather than working**: the Falco and Mazza archives sit on southern Italian ground and the same walk would be their whole first week. Recorded here as a decision so that the next session does not re-open it.

rows.what: The towns of our people, as a switch on the research map
rows.note: A second layer on the research map that is not about books at all: **160 towns, 956 placements of documented people, 106 of the towns outside Croatia** — Torrington, Memphis, Pfullingen, Broken Hill, Brisbane. Lifted whole out of `atlas.json` rather than geocoded a second time, stripped of its film lists so no register is offered twice, and **switched off by default** with a violet filter button that turns it on. 43 towns carry both a people marker and a shelf marker.

rows.what: Three maps merged into one, at /map/
rows.note: The research map, the atlas and the graves map were three maps of the same ground with three geocoders and three legends. **1,235 + 160 + 64 markers are 1,358 places**; 84 answer more than one of the three questions and **12 answer all three**. The colour switches between the questions; the panel never does. `/research-map/`, `/atlas/` and `/graves-map/` redirect.

rows.what: Towns for the living relatives
rows.note: The living rule changed on 15 September: **name and town, never a date**. **All eleven living people the archive names are now placed** — David and Cheryl at Johannesburg and Brisbane; Cristina, Alessio and Mateo at Brisbane; **Ada, Horst, Mark, Gayle, Nicole and Kirsten at Johannesburg**, on David's word of the same day. Robbie — deceased, no date held — is placed at Johannesburg too, marked **inferred**: his wife and both his daughters are there and nothing in the archive names a town for him.

rows.what: The Brisbane Mario stood twice in the roster
rows.note:
**Folded into one row.** He was **Mario De Franceschi 1938–2013** off a Find a Grave memorial and **Mario Defranceschi 1938–2013** out of MyHeritage 4507883 — two slugs under `/who/`, two dots in Brisbane, one man. The surviving row carries both spellings and both sources.

**The heading on this row was wrong twice over.** It said «David's father», which is what the mis-flagged rows had made this archive believe; his father is **Ivan Anton Defranceski, 1951–2026**. [Correction 79](/corrections/).

rows.what: Antony De Franceski of Willowbank — is he the Horsham family?
rows.note: **Answered: yes.** He is **Anton Mario De Franceski**, born 21 August 1944 at Reutlingen — Zdravko and Ruža's only child, four years old on the *General M B Stewart*. Eight NAA items say so, including **A11534, 58–60**, which carries all three dates of birth in one line, and **D4881**, his own arrival card, which gives the middle name and the Australian spelling. Two corrections came out of it: he was four on the ship and not nine, and «Zorafko» at Horsham is Zdravko, so that is one burial and not two.

rows.what: Order NAA D4881 — Anton Mario De Franceski's arrival card, and run Ryerson
rows.note: The card runs **13 April 1949 to 31 December 1976** and is held at Adelaide; it should carry addresses, and it is the cheapest route to how a Horsham boy ended up at Ipswich. **Ryerson Index** — free, covers Australian death notices for 1999 — was returning «Server Overloaded» on 15 September and needs another run; a funeral notice would name a wife and children, and would settle the two-year gap between the cemetery's age and four documents.

rows.what: Rebuild the roster from the live MyHeritage tree, not the 2018 GEDCOM
rows.note: **The roster's family-file source is a GEDCOM of July 2018 — 8,286 people. The live tree has 15,643.** A note of 7 September already said the export was retired and read 459 individuals of the surname out of the live tree; **that reading was never imported**. The Australian branch went in on 15 September — fifteen people — because David asked why his cousin's sister at Horsham was missing. **The rest of the tree is still outstanding**, and every one of the 513 roster rows carrying a 2018 identifier needs checking against it.

rows.what: Anka Nera Defranceski, dead at Belgrade in 1944, aged twenty-nine
rows.note:
Born at Crikvenica in 1915, married name **Oreščanin**, died at **Belgrade in 1944**. That is the whole of it. A Croatian woman of twenty-nine dying in occupied Belgrade in 1944 is a question, not a fact — and this archive has never asked it. Arolsen, the Belgrade city registry and the Yugoslav victims' census are the places to start.

**The tree adds two husbands and deepens the question.** **Josip Geiger, 1911–1936**, dead at twenty-five when she was twenty-one; then **Branko Oreščanin**, whose name she carries. And **her mother Ursula died at Belgrade too, in 1975** — two women of one family dead in that city, thirty-one years apart. There is now a second surname to search Arolsen and the Yugoslav victims' census on.

**Arolsen searched on 16 September and she is not in it.** No person record for *Defranceski Anka*; no match under Oreščanin or Geiger either. Her brothers are all over that archive — **the surname returns 79 person records** — and she is not, which says she died at Belgrade outside the German system. **The Belgrade city registry and the Yugoslav victims' census are what is left.**

*And the 79 is a finding on its own*: this archive has read exactly one Arolsen file.

rows.what: David's call: the children on the map
rows.note: Three living children of the Australian branch are now named on the map with no dates and a town — **Charlotte Rita Baviello, Louis Hendy and Lewis Rose**, alongside Alessio and Mateo. That follows the rule as David set it: name and town, never a date. **They are other people's children rather than David's**, and if he would rather they were not named at all, it is one line to take them off.

rows.what: Pull the live tree — 798 of the surname, not 459
rows.note:
**Walked, counted, and then blocked on the pipe.** Following the tree's own family links outward instead of querying given names found **798 individuals of the surname — 339 more than the name queries did — and 313 of them carry a citation David typed in by hand.**

**The crawl cannot deliver them.** MyHeritage blocks a POST to a local receiver and the browser tool channel truncates at about a thousand characters, which is ten people a call. **A GEDCOM export of tree 4 is one click**, and it is exactly what the retired 2018 file was. [Written up as an errand](/errands/).

What the walk did deliver on the way past is on [the search register](/searched/): Ursula dying at Belgrade, Robbie born at Senj, and four more places the archive had wrong or missing.

rows.what: Walk every live-tree person's Facts panel for the citation text David typed by hand
rows.note:
`facts[].additionalContent` carries the **full source citation** — FamilySearch ark URLs, film and image numbers, archive names — entered by David himself. **211 of 459 people carry one.** It is the most sourced material in this whole estate and none of it is on the site.

**Counted on 15 September: 313 of the 798 carry one.** They come out of the same GEDCOM as everything else, so this waits on the same one click.

rows.what: Search the live tree for misspellings of the surname — Lisa was one letter short
rows.note:
**One typo, one person.** *Defraneski* returns Lisa and nothing else; *De Francesci, Defrancheski, Defranceshi, Defrancesky, Defranchesci, Defrancesci* and *Franzeschini* all return zero. The blind spot was real and it was one letter wide.

Sideways find: **Franceschini** returns a Brazilian-forename group — Aurelio 1892, Turno 1894, Aristeu 1901, Tosca 1907 — which belongs with [Trentino](/trentino/).

rows.what: List every placeholder node in the live tree, and the unconnected clusters behind them
rows.note: **Read, and it is better than the row predicted.** David built a node called **«PLACEHOLDERS Defranceschi's for Investigation (not real)»** with **twenty-three children, one per country**, and under the Croatian one **seventeen more, one per town** — including Gologorica and Gračišće. Australia is filed by state, and **Mario of Brisbane hangs under QLD**: David had filed him as unconnected himself, years before this archive claimed him and had to take it back. [Published on the diaspora page](/diaspora/).

rows.what: Audit every roster row flagged «mine» against the direct line
rows.note: **Run, and twelve rows failed it.** The test is written down for the first time: *«mine» means this archive can NAME the path from this person to David* — a place on the direct line, a named relationship, or a household the archive has drawn. A shared surname on a gravestone is not a path. Twelve Find a Grave memorials came off the flag — Millbrook, the Bronx, East Farmingdale, Middle Village, Hartsdale, and the Lilydale, Fawkner and Parkville Italians the diaspora page had already filed under a different migration. **187 rows keep it.** [Correction 80](/corrections/).

rows.what: Put the live tree in the sources table and mark the 2018 GEDCOM superseded
rows.note: **Done.** [About](/about/) now carries the live tree as a source in its own right — 15,643 people, tree 4, read 7 and 15 September — and the July 2018 export is marked **SUPERSEDED** in its own title, with the reason on it.

rows.what: Make every builder fail loudly when its gazetteer is missing
rows.note: **Done: `scripts/gazcheck.py`.** Every map builder now dies with a message naming the path it was given when its gazetteer comes back short. Tested with a wrong directory: exit 2, nothing written.

rows.what: A regression guard: a builder that places fewer places than last time must say so
rows.note: **Done, in the same file.** A builder that places fewer places than its own last output refuses to write and says by how many. `--allow-shrink` is there for a fall that is real and intended.

rows.what: Petar Vid's German household — Ursula, Renate, and Luise Salzer
rows.note: **Named, and there are three children rather than two.** **Ursula (Korn), born at Urach 1940; Renata (Buck), born at Metzingen 1945; and Peter**, whom the Arolsen cards do not mention at all. Their mother is **Luise Salzer, born 1919**. All three are living — eighty-six, eighty-one, and undated — and are on the archive now by name and town, which the present rule allows and the old one did not.

rows.what: Koka Defranceski — Ivan Anton's second wife, a name and nothing else
rows.note: **Asked, and the answer is that there is no answer in the tree.** She is a spouse node with **no dates, no places, no children and no maiden name**; «Koka» is a pet name. She is on the roster now as exactly that, and [as an open question](/open-questions/) — David's grandfather had twenty-six years at Senj after the divorce and this is the only trace of them.

rows.what: Hedviga — Blažević or Codron?
rows.note:
**Codron is a later husband, not a maiden name.** Hedviga married **Santou (Shemtov) Isaac Codron, 1913–1997**, and the tree names a third husband, **Ladislav Carr**; her parents are Ljubomir Blažević and Milka Papić.

**And the question paid for itself twice over.** She reached South Africa in **April 1975, from Zimbabwe** — a whole leg of this family's journey that no page of this archive had — and her birth date is settled at **3 August 1926**, where the archive had carried two transposed dates and preferred neither.

rows.what: Order NAA B44 V1978/151 and V1978/152 — Zdravko and Ruža's naturalisation
rows.note: Naturalisation at Melbourne in **1978**, twenty-nine years after they landed and a year before he died. A naturalisation file carries **address, occupation, arrival particulars and a photograph**, and this archive has none of those for either of them. Access status «not yet examined», which means it has to be asked for before it can be read.

rows.what: Check whether NAA A2571 and B78 are digitised before paying for a copy
rows.note:
**Checked, and the answer is none of them.** All eight items are **«Open» and not digitised** — A11534, both B44 naturalisations, the three A2571 alien registrations and the two B78 cards. «Open» in RecordSearch means readable, not scanned, which is exactly the distinction this check existed to draw.

**It turns the whole Australian side of this family from a search into an order**, and the two B44 files are still «not yet examined», so access has to be applied for before a copy can be. They should go in one request rather than eight.

rows.what: Victorian death registrations for Zdravko 1979 and Ruža 1996
rows.note:
**Turned into an errand rather than a search, because it was never a search.** The free Victorian index returns a name, a year and a registration number; **the parents are on the certificate**, which has to be applied and paid for. Zdravko's 1979 death is inside the open window and is [written up as an errand](/errands/); **Ruža's 1996 death is not** — Victoria releases deaths at thirty years.

Separately: the BDM search form could not be driven from either browser here. Its Angular model ignores values set programmatically, and real typing needs a browser pane this session does not have. One minute of David's own browser.

rows.what: The Commonwealth Gazette naturalisation notices of 1978, free on Trove
rows.note: Australian naturalisations were **published by name in the Commonwealth of Australia Gazette**, and Trove holds the Gazette. It would confirm NAA B44 without ordering it, and it gives the **town of residence** at the moment of the oath.

rows.what: Trove: the Wimmera Mail-Times and the Horsham papers from 1949
rows.note: **Run, and the answer is nothing — weakly.** No result for the surname in Trove's newspapers across the 1940s or the 1950s. **Trove's newspaper digitisation mostly stops in 1954** and whether the *Wimmera Mail-Times* is held for 1949–54 has not been established, so this rules out the easy version and not much more. [On the search register](/searched/).

rows.what: Ruža's parents — Lovre Hreljac and Dragica Vlahović of Fužine
rows.note:
Both are in the live tree, **both deceased, and neither is in this archive**. Ruža was born at **Fužine on 13 February 1922** — her own town certificate says so against a single Arolsen entry that reads 2 May — and a second place, **Belnica**, appears on the Neuhausen list. The Hreljac line enters this family through her and has never been opened.

**Checked 15 September: Fužine's films stop at 1889** and Ruža was born in 1922, so her own baptism is not on any film this archive can reach. Her parents Lovre and Dragica married before that, though, and **Fužine marriages 1778–1857 and births 1725–1889 are clickable from the map** — that is where to look for the Hreljac household, not for her.

rows.what: Fužine and Belnica — are they on the map at all?
rows.note: **Both answered.** Fužine is on the map with **five volumes, all of them now clickable** — births 1725–1778, 1778–1857 and 1858–1889, marriages 1778–1857, deaths to 1916 — and it is in the main Croatian collection, not in Delnice. **Belnica is on no catalogue this archive holds** and is not on the map; it is a hamlet rather than a parish, and whatever it means on Ruža's Neuhausen entry it is not a register office.

rows.what: Crikvenica 1909–1926 — one roll holds all five baptisms
rows.note:
**Answered, and it is an order rather than a search.** FamilySearch's Crikvenica films are cut at **Rođeni 1896** — the hundred-year line as it stood when they were made — so all five children of Anton Rudolf and Ursula were born after the end of the only collection this archive can reach for free.

**They are all on one reel.** HR-HDA-1448, **R 1909–1926, roll ZM-34J/362, mark M-6957**, Matični ured Crikvenica, digitised: Josip Petar 1911, Petar Vid 1913, Anka Nera 1915, Zdravko 1921 and Ivan Anton 1925. Written up as [an errand](/errands/) with the Status animarum and the 1909–1947 marriages, which come off the same collection and should go in one request.

**Crikvenica births 1897–1908 are in neither collection** — that stretch holds Ruža Jarmacki born 1903 and the POLD… of the monument, and it needs the parish office or the Rijeka archdiocesan archive.

rows.what: Anton Rudolf's exact death date, 1943
rows.note:
The archive and the tree both say **«circa 1943, Crikvenica»**. His son Zdravko was taken by the Partisans that same year. A death in occupied Croatia in 1943 with no date is a gap worth closing, and the Crikvenica death register is the place it closes.

**Checked: it cannot be searched, only asked for.** Crikvenica deaths on film stop at **1908**; the 1943 register sits with the **Matični ured**, and [the errand](/errands/) for it has been standing since before this session. The same office holds the 1909–1926 births.

rows.what: Why the family left Gračišće for the Kvarner coast
rows.note: **Josip Defranceschi, generation 4 — Gračišće to Crikvenica.** The archive draws the move and has never explained it. It is the second unexplained jump in the line, after Mione to Gologorica, and unlike the first one it happens inside the nineteenth century with registers on both ends.

rows.what: Klenovica, house 22
rows.note: Anton Rudolf is **«born 20 January 1890, Ledenice / Klenovica 22»**. A house number is an address the land registers and the church's *status animarum* can both be searched on, and this archive has done neither. It is the Kvarner equivalent of Gologorica's house 17.

rows.what: Senj to the front of the ark queue
rows.note: **Overtaken.** The harvest finished the whole queue before a priority order was worth building — all 5,482 volumes are linkable, Senj's fifteen among them. Worth doing if the queue is ever regenerated at that size again; not worth doing now.

rows.what: Populate the per-volume read ledger from the search register
rows.note: **Done — four volumes pinned, and six places now have a book of their own opened instead of two.** Gračišće's baptism book 1667–1745 and Donji Proložac's deaths 1837–1859 are **read right through**; Svetvinčenat's 1663–1708 and Vodnjan's 1815–1884 reel are **read in part**. «Part read» now counts as started.

rows.what: Say in one line what was read at each of the twenty teal places
rows.note: **Done.** A teal marker prints the rows themselves under a heading that says not one of them is a volume from the shelf above. Žminj shows *«Libri žminjski, libar drugi (Žminj 2008) — partial»*; a place with more than twelve says how many more.

rows.what: The forty burials with no parish named
rows.note:
**Attempted, and the route is now written down.** They cannot be placed from anything in this repository. The burial rows carry a name, a year and a place-string that is only ever «Croazia, Austria», «Hrvatska, Österreich», «Regnum Croatiae» or «Kraljevina Hrvatska» — **and no ark**. Joining them to `register.json` on name and year matches seventeen of the forty and gains nothing, because that file carries the same raw index place.

**The resolution already exists as a method** and this archive has run it on all 954 indexed records: every persona carries the ark of the image it was read from, the ark resolves to a **DGS film number**, and the catalogue names the film's parish. It is what turned eighteen known parishes into [ninety-three](/istria-sweep/). **But only the aggregate survived** — 93 rows of parish, count and span. The per-record output was never written to disk.

**So the job is: re-harvest those forty personas with their arks, and resolve each one.** Half a day, and it would put a quarter of everything this archive knows about its dead onto the map.

rows.what: /map/ at phone width
rows.note: **Checked at 375px and it holds** — scrollWidth equals clientWidth, so nothing pushes the page sideways. One fix made: the three question buttons size to their own text, which made a ragged left edge on a phone, so below 640px they go full width.

rows.what: Retire the hand-kept coordinates in atlas-seed.json
rows.note: **Done by building `data/gazetteer.json`** — 2,456 places distilled from the GeoNames dumps by `scripts/build-gazetteer.py` and committed, so no builder needs the seventy-seven megabytes of dumps to run. The atlas gained six places by it. The seed keeps only what a gazetteer genuinely cannot resolve, and says so.

rows.what: The `/tmp/harvest-geo.json` dependency
rows.note: **Gone.** `build-atlas.py` reads the committed gazetteer; the seventeen hand-checked places the old file carried have been folded in and marked as hand-checked. The file is read if it happens to be there and nothing breaks when it is not.

rows.what: Senj, 1926 and 1948 — Hedviga's birth and the marriage
rows.note: **Hedviga «Seka» Blažević was born at Senj in 1926 and married Ivan Anton there**; both registers are with the Matični ured, past the end of every film. [The errand is drafted](/errands/) and waits on David's own details, like the DAPA forms. The live tree carries her as **«Blažević (Codron)»**, which implies a marriage this archive has never heard of — the same register would settle that too.

rows.what: Camillo's own books, and the Istrian bundle
rows.note: Nine printed titles stand pending on [the search register](/searched/) and they are the **secondary literature of this family's own historian**: Camillo's *Storia documentata della Contea di Pisino* and *Povijest Pazinske knežije*, Carlo's *Uspomene*, Bertoša's two, Jelinčić, Gentileo's bibliography, the 1788 visitation and the *Atti e memorie* obituary. **Four of them are one order from the Pula university library.** They are the cheapest unexploited body of material the archive has.

rows.what: Corsica — is Tomino's Defranceschi household in Vergé-Franceschi?
rows.note: **Vergé-Franceschi's «Le cap Corse: généalogies et destins» (2006)** is the reference work for Cap Corse families, and the archive holds four Corsican graves at **Tomino and Mandolacce**. It would settle in one afternoon whether that household is a fourth population of the surname or a branch with a route to it. Not yet obtained.

rows.what: Test FamilySearch's full-text search — it has never been tried
rows.note:
Listed as **«untested»** on the search register and left there. FamilySearch's full-text search reads the **handwriting of unindexed images**, which is precisely the state of every Croatian register this archive has catalogued: 5,489 volumes, none of them name-indexed. **If it works on Istrian parish hands it changes the shape of this whole archive.** One afternoon to find out.

**Blocked on 16 September: the FamilySearch session is signed out.** Full-text search redirects to the login page and the persona API stopped answering at the same time. **This archive does not enter credentials.** One sign-in from David and this runs.

rows.what: The two letters drafted and never sent
rows.note: **`requests/arolsen-td-349822.md`** — the Arolsen tracing case that stood open on Petar for thirty years, eight documents withheld online. **`requests/nsk-de-franceschi-archive.md`** — the De Franceschi archive at the National and University Library. Both are written and waiting on a signature.

rows.what: The four Adriatic archive enquiries that are written and unsent
rows.note: Udine's **Notarile antico B. 2979**; the **Veritas register** for the *Aquilone*; the **«Famiglia Franceschi»** notice in *Il Rammentatore zaratino* 1859; and the Vienna **Haus-, Hof- und Staatsarchiv** correspondence of December 1918 naming a «Dr Defranceschi». Each is drafted on [the errands page](/errands/) and each needs the same thing: a name and an address on the form.

rows.what: The five Croatian and Brazilian archives with a search standing open
rows.note: Rijeka **HR-DARI-382 kut. 1**; Zadar's **Prijamni ured**; **Bakar's parish registers**; the **Stemmi della nobiltà di Buccari**; **Stare hrvatske novine** at dnc.nsk.hr; the **Arolsen online collections**; and the **Museu da Imigração** at São Paulo. Seven rows on the search register that say *pending* and have said it for a week. Several are free and online and simply have not been opened.

rows.what: Hand the Blažević family to the Blažević archive
rows.note:
**Handed over on [the Senj line page](/senj-line/)**, named and dated and not written up: her parents **Ljubomir 1892–1966** and **Milka 1886–1971**, and six siblings — Leo 1920–2008, Karmela «Carmen» 1922–1987, **Oto 1923–1945**, Ljubomir 1929–2007, Mario 1933–1984, Anton.

**What belongs here is the join, which is Hedviga.** The rest is [the Blažević Archive's](https://daviddef.github.io/TheBlazevic/) ground, and a second family reconstructed on a page about a different surname is how an estate ends up with two versions of one person.

rows.what: Read the twenty-three placeholder pens, country by country
rows.note:
**Walked: forty-nine nodes and 160 named people inside them**, counted pen by pen and [published as a table](/diaspora/). **Brazil 22, the United States 19, Italy 18, Croatia 16, Austria 14, Venezuela 10** — and Brazil being the largest is exactly what this archive had already written from the other direction.

**None of the 160 is in the roster.** Reading each of them properly — name by name, against the records — is the next thing, and it is a body of work rather than a row.

rows.what: The 160 in the pens, name by name
rows.note:
The pens are counted; **the people in them are not read**. 160 named individuals, sorted by country, that David could not join and this archive has never tested.

**Start with the two that are cheapest and closest**: the **South Africa** pen — Rosemary Marie Michele and Maude De Franceschi, in the country this family spent thirty years in — and the **Croatia** pen, whose sixteen are already sorted by town and can be tested straight against [the map](/map/). **Brazil's twenty-two** are the largest group and the one this archive has the least ability to check.

rows.what: Seventy-nine Arolsen records under the surname, and one read
rows.note:
Searching Arolsen for Anka Nera turned up the number sideways: **79 person records under DEFRANCESKI**, and this archive has read **one file** — the family's own, ITS D-1.505, and that only because the family held copies.

**Four of the visible names are Anton and one is Lujza**, which is Luise Salzer; the rest are unexamined. Arolsen's online collections are free and indexed by name. **This is one of the cheapest bodies of unread material the archive has**, and the reason it was never opened is that nobody counted it.

close: **Four things are waiting on people rather than on searching**: Ovaro's undigitised registers, the Y-DNA test, the three archive request forms that need David's own data, and a 404 page that belongs to another session. Everything else here is either finished or is a book that can be opened tonight.
